analysis.one_liner: Gives farmworkers pandemic hazard pay, paid sick leave, and job protections.
analysis.headline: Sponsored by six Democratic senators, the bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing or vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required farms, ranches, and food producers that accept federal coronavirus aid to give their workers emergency paid sick leave and $13 an hour in hazard pay, capped at $10,000 per worker, with the money flowing through Agriculture Department grants. It also would have limited layoffs of farmworkers during the emergency, required compliance with CDC safety guidelines, and given small producers grants for handwashing stations, portable restrooms, and protective equipment.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmworkers and food production workers — field hands, meatpackers, cannery workers — including those regardless of citizenship or immigration status. Workers who caught the virus and died would have left a lump-sum payment to their next of kin.

how_it_helps.text: Covered agricultural employers would have to provide emergency paid sick leave — 80 hours for full-time workers — during the pandemic period and 90 days after the public health emergency ends, without regard to employer size or immigration status.

Workers would receive premium pay of $13 for every hour worked, up to $10,000 per worker ($5,000 for those earning $100,000 or more), paid for by USDA grants rather than by the employer's own funds, with employers barred from cutting existing pay or hours to offset it.
If a worker showed coronavirus symptoms and died of the disease during the covered period, the employer would pay a lump sum of the remaining premium pay to the worker's next of kin.

The Labor Department would write rules limiting involuntary furloughs or terminations of farmworkers during the covered period, and violations could be enforced through Labor Department action and private lawsuits, including class actions that forced-arbitration agreements could not block.
Producers with 50 or fewer employees would get grants of $500 per worker to buy handwashing stations, portable restrooms, and personal protective equipment meeting CDC guidelines.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the premium pay grants, designated as emergency spending with no dollar ceiling. Employers bear compliance costs, keep records, and cannot reduce existing wages or benefits, though tax credits offset sick-leave costs for employers with 500 or fewer employees.

drawbacks.text: The premium pay grants are funded by unlimited emergency appropriations — the bill appropriates 'such sums as are necessary' for every eligible producer that applies, with no total cost estimate attached.

Coverage is tied to funding, not risk: only workers at producers that receive federal agriculture-specific coronavirus funding are covered, so equally exposed workers at producers that did not take such aid would get no sick leave or hazard pay.
Violations carry no criminal penalties; they are treated as civil wage violations under the Fair Labor Standards Act, which limits the deterrent for repeat offenders.

Employers absorbing federal aid would face new mandates on pay, layoffs, recordkeeping, and daily temperature checks and symptom screening, costs an honest supporter would acknowledge even with the grants offsetting the hazard pay itself.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — federally funded hazard pay and sick leave for some of the lowest-paid, most exposed workers in the economy — outweighs the costs, which are largely taxpayer dollars routed to those same workers through their employers. The design flaw is that eligibility hinges on whether the employer took federal aid, leaving comparable unprotected workers outside the bill, and the open-ended appropriation was written without a cost ceiling.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or brought it to a vote, and the bill died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Jeff Merkley introduced the bill on June 23, 2020, joined by Sens. Blumenthal, Sanders, Harris, Warren, and Leahy.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day — the only action it ever received.
No further committee action, hearing, or floor vote occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Agricultural employers that accepted federal coronavirus aid kept receiving it without the paid sick leave, hazard pay, or job-security strings this bill would have attached; the farmworkers it covered got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agricultural employers taking federal COVID aid

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; all six sponsors were Democrats plus one Independent, and no Republican cosponsored.

industries.industry: Agricultural employers (growers, ranchers, and food processors taking federal COVID farm aid)
industries.note: The bill would have handed them USDA grants covering the $13-per-hour hazard pay for their workers, but imposed sick-leave obligations, anti-layoff rules, daily CDC screening requirements, and civil liability enforceable by workers in court. Their interest in taking federal aid without those strings ran against the workers the bill protected.
Contractors providing or paying farmworkers would have had to accept grant pass-through conditions and could be held liable for failing to pay the required premium pay.
